title: Growth rate and peak height
question: Per season, does the slope r of ln(ILI+) in the growth window predict the season's peak ILI+?

hypotheses.statement: A larger early growth rate r goes with a higher peak ILI+.
hypotheses.null: The peak ILI+ is unrelated to r.

hypotheses.statement: A larger growth rate brings the peak earlier in the season.
hypotheses.null: The peak week is unrelated to r.

concepts.label: Growth rate r
concepts.description: Slope of ln(ILI+) per week in the growth window.

concepts.label: Effective reproduction number
concepts.description: R = (1 + r·Tg/k)^k with Tg = 3 days, k = 4.
concepts.why: Links r to the SIR model.

concepts.label: Circulating subtype
concepts.description: A(H3N2), A(H1N1)pdm09 or B dominating a season.
concepts.why: A confounder: H3N2 seasons tend to be more severe.

strategy.detail: Subtype counts per week from CDC FluView public-health labs (Delphi fluview_clinical has A and B only: total_a, total_b).

concepts.label: Prior immunity
concepts.description: Share immune at the season start (vaccination, earlier infection).
concepts.why: Sets the effective R and the peak.

strategy.detail: Vaccination coverage per season (CDC FluVaxView): misses immunity from infection.

issues.text: Only eight seasons have lab data and enough influenza in this source (2016–17 on, without 2020–22), so a regression has few points.
issues.fix: Read the slope's interval, not only its sign; expand with regional series (Delphi has HHS regions and states) for more points.

issues.text: Seasons differ in subtype, timing and prior immunity, which move both r and the peak.
issues.fix: Name subtype and immunity as confounders; the association is what the data shows.

alternatives.question: Within one season, do the ten HHS regions with faster growth peak higher?
alternatives.why: Drill down: more points with the same virus.

alternatives.question: Do seasons dominated by influenza B grow more slowly than A seasons?
alternatives.why: Expand: share_b per season is on the board.

data.request: Weekly counts of A(H3N2), A(H1N1)pdm09 and B per season, national.

method.summary: Regress peak on r_week across seasons (one row per season of the seasons table).

steps.title: Fit the growth window
steps.detail: growth: r_week per season from ln(ILI+) between 5% and 60% of the peak, before it.

steps.title: Convert r to R
steps.detail: seasons: R = (1 + r·Tg/k)^k, Tg 3 days, k 4; herd threshold, final size, peak prevalence.

steps.title: Regress peak on r_week
steps.detail: Across the seasons table; and peak_t on r_week for H2.

steps.title: Read against the SIR prediction
steps.detail: SIR says higher R, higher and earlier peak; check the sign and size of b.

caveats: ILI+ is a proxy for incidence, not a count of infections; its scale depends on who visits sentinel providers.
R depends on the assumed generation interval (3 days here): a longer one gives a larger R for the same r.
The growth window is a rule (5–60% of the peak), and seasons with two waves (2019–20) or an early start (2022–23) fit less well: read fit_r2.
SIR assumes a homogeneous, well-mixed population; school terms and holidays bend real curves (the Christmas dip).
Eight seasons: a correlation is weak evidence.
